document.description: bcoE-bcoF (cdhAB, SMc01638) encodes a bifunctional cytoplasmic enzyme of Sinorhizobium meliloti L-carnitine catabolism. The N-terminal region (residues 1-335, 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase family) oxidizes L-carnitine to 3-dehydrocarnitine with NAD(+), and the C-terminal hotdog-fold region (residues 336-496) hydrolyzes betainyl-CoA (N,N,N-trimethylglycyl-CoA) to glycine betaine and CoA, so one polypeptide carries the first and last steps of the route whose middle step is the BcoG cleavage enzyme. In Pseudomonas the two activities are separate proteins (CdhA and CdhB). The purified homodimer was characterized kinetically, and gene disruption abolishes growth on gamma-butyrobetaine, which S. meliloti converts to carnitine before degrading it.

review.reason: The HAMAP-based location fits a soluble NAD(+)-dependent dehydrogenase without signal peptide or transmembrane segment acting on intracellular carnitine.

review.summary: Same location transferred from the Rhizobium sp. bifunctional ortholog.
InterPro2GO transfer from the 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase domains; the enzyme acts on carnitine.
review.reason: Both activities act in carnitine catabolism; neither substrate is a fatty acid or fatty acyl-CoA. The domain mapping fits the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of the family, not the L-carnitine dehydrogenase subfamily.

supported_by.supporting_text: Multifunctional enzyme that catalyzes the NAD(+)-dependent oxidation of L-carnitine to 3-dehydrocarnitine and the cleavage of betainyl-CoA (N,N,N-trimethylglycyl-CoA) into glycine betaine and coenzyme A (PubMed:30670548).

source_defects.explanation: InterPro2GO maps IPR006108/IPR006176 (3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase domains) to fatty acid metabolic process; the L-carnitine dehydrogenase subfamily (IPR026578) shares the domains but not the fatty acid substrate.

review.summary: Correct but less specific than carnitine catabolic process.
review.reason: Both activities act in the degradative direction, allowing growth on carnitine as sole carbon and nitrogen source; the specific child GO:0042413 is proposed below as a NEW row.

supported_by.supporting_text: Is involved in a L- carnitine degradation pathway that allows R.meliloti to grow on L- carnitine as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen (PubMed:30670548).

review.summary: Rhea-mapped activity of the C-terminal betainyl-CoA thioesterase region; the closest GO term for EC 3.1.2.33.
review.reason: The purified enzyme hydrolyzes betainyl-CoA with high efficiency (kcat 142 s-1); GO has no betainyl-CoA-specific term (see proposed_new_terms), so this parent is the most precise available. The enzyme also hydrolyzes L-carnitinyl-CoA, but at kcat 0.9 s-1 against 142.3 s-1 for betainyl-CoA at the same KM of 12 uM, a 158-fold difference in turnover; UniProt itself calls this "much lower efficiency". On the promiscuous-activity tiers in projects/ENZYME_SPECIFICITY.md that reads as in vitro activity of unknown physiological relevance rather than a second evolved function: no carnitinyl-CoA ligase is known in this pathway, so there is no route by which the substrate would be formed in vivo. GO:0016289 covers both reactions, so no separate row is proposed; the open question is recorded in suggested_questions.

supported_by.supporting_text: Reaction=N,N,N-trimethylglycyl-CoA + H2O = glycine betaine + CoA + H(+);
Can also hydrolyze L-carnitinyl-CoA, but with much lower efficiency (PubMed:30670548).

review.reason: The specific descendant GO:0047728 is supported experimentally for this protein.

review.summary: Electronic row for the experimentally established activity.
Correct cofactor binding; NAD+ binding is the specific child already on this gene.
review.reason: NAD(+) is the oxidant of the dehydrogenase reaction and the HAMAP-defined site binds NAD(+).

review.summary: Cofactor binding by the N-terminal Rossmann domain; subsidiary to the catalytic activity.
review.reason: The term is as precise as warranted but describes cofactor binding, not either of the two catalytic activities.

review.summary: Proposed: the enzyme catalyzes two steps of carnitine breakdown, and its disruption abolishes growth on gamma-butyrobetaine.
review.reason: Both activities are steps of L-carnitine degradation to glycine betaine, and the mutant cannot use gamma-butyrobetaine, which S. meliloti converts to carnitine before degrading it. The specific catabolic term is absent from GOA for this entry.

supported_by.supporting_text: Is involved in a L- carnitine degradation pathway that allows R.meliloti to grow on L- carnitine as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen (PubMed:30670548).
DISRUPTION PHENOTYPE: Disruption of the gene in strain Rm2011 abolishes growth on gamma-butyrobetaine (GBB).

findings.statement: All enzymes converting gamma-butyrobetaine through L-carnitine to glycine betaine in S. meliloti were characterized in vitro; the gene cluster is conserved in several bacterial classes.
findings.supporting_text: The conservation of l-carnitine metabolism genes in different bacterial taxonomic classes underscores the role of l-carnitine as a ubiquitous nutrient.

reference_review.review_notes: Abstract-only cache (PMC6416908 full text not retrievable here); the kinetics and disruption phenotype are taken from the curated UniProt entry, which cites this paper with experimental evidence.

core_functions.description: N-terminal region: NAD(+)-dependent oxidation of L-carnitine to 3-dehydrocarnitine, the first step of aerobic L-carnitine catabolism.
C-terminal region: hydrolysis of betainyl-CoA to glycine betaine and CoA (EC 3.1.2.33), the last step of the route.

supported_by.supporting_text: Reaction=N,N,N-trimethylglycyl-CoA + H2O = glycine betaine + CoA + H(+);

proposed_new_terms.proposed_definition: Catalysis of the reaction: N,N,N-trimethylglycyl-CoA + H2O = glycine betaine + CoA + H+.
proposed_new_terms.justification: EC 3.1.2.33 (RHEA:45716) is measured for this enzyme and for P. aeruginosa CdhB; GO has only the broader acyl-CoA hydrolase term.

supported_by.supporting_text: Reaction=N,N,N-trimethylglycyl-CoA + H2O = glycine betaine + CoA + H(+);

suggested_questions.question: Is the C-terminal thioesterase region homologous to the stand-alone CdhB hotdog thioesterases of Pseudomonas, and did the fusion arise once in Rhizobiales and Roseobacter lineages?
Is L-carnitinyl-CoA ever formed in S. meliloti, or is the 158-fold slower hydrolysis of it by this enzyme purely an in vitro property of a pocket evolved for betainyl-CoA?

suggested_experiments.description: Express the two regions separately and test whether each retains its activity, and whether the fusion channels betainyl-CoA formed by BcoG.
suggested_experiments.experiment_type: protein dissection and coupled enzyme assay
